title: Getting a Head Start
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Using the story of Robert Taylor and Minnetonka's Softsoap brand, this article illustrates how a small company secured a lasting competitive advantage by cornering the supply of liquid-soap pump dispensers before rivals could copy the product. The piece generalizes the lesson to any leader or team pursuing a first-mover advantage: identifying the resources and relationships that create a real head start, then organizing them in advance so execution can move quickly once the decision is made. It cautions that speed alone isn't enough — being early without strategic execution can lead to over-investment in an unrealistic commitment. The takeaway is that sustainable head starts come from preparation, not just enthusiasm.
points: Robert Taylor's Softsoap company secured a two-year market lead by buying up the entire U.S. supply of pump dispensers before competitors could react.
First-mover advantages include setting standards, building deeper relationships, negotiating better terms, and expanding timelines.
Getting ahead requires organizing resources and relationships in advance so execution can happen quickly once the decision is made.
Being early without strategic execution risks over-investment or an unrealistic commitment to a project.
quotes: He believed that even a small company could compete with the largest consumer product companies if it had the best product and could get a head start.
Taylor spent $12 million to purchase 100 million pump dispensers from the only two U.S. manufacturers at the time.
The Softsoap brand quickly dominated the market and established itself as a household name before the competitors could retaliate.
Getting a head start is an essential leadership strategy in any organization or team, no matter what the idea, service, product, or initiative.
When people and resources are behind you, getting a head start is relatively easy.
